title: Mixture / Truncated Distribution Fit
variableSelected: Select a variable that contains the distribution
label1: Fits a mixture of normal distributions (e.g. bimodal data), a truncated normal distribution, or both together (a truncated mixture). For a single, non-truncated, non-mixture distribution with formal goodness-of-fit p-values, use the 'Distribution Fit P-value' dialog instead.
mixtureChk: Fit as a mixture of normal distributions (e.g. bimodal data)
mixtureEngineLabel: Component-count selection (ignored if 'Truncate' below is checked, or if 'Fit as a mixture' above is unchecked)
mixtoolsEngine: Fixed number of components (specify the number)
autoEngine: Automatically select the number of components (tries 2 up to the maximum, keeps the lowest BIC)
startingMeans: Starting mean values per component, comma-separated (optional - leave blank to auto-initialize)
bootSEChk: Compute bootstrap standard errors (adds computation time)
plotChk: Show histogram with fitted density overlay

help.title: Mixture / Truncated Distribution Fit
help.body:
Description
Fits a normal distribution to data under one of four scenarios, selected by the two checkboxes on this dialog:
  • Neither checked: a single, non-truncated normal distribution (provided for completeness; the 'Distribution Fit P-value' dialog offers formal KS/CvM/AD goodness-of-fit p-values for this case and many other distribution families, and is the better choice for a single-distribution fit).
  • Mixture only: a mixture of two or more normal distributions (e.g. bimodal, trimodal data), fit by the EM algorithm via mixtools::normalmixEM. You can either fix the number of components yourself, or let the dialog try several component counts and keep the one with the lowest BIC.
  • Truncate only: a single normal distribution restricted to a bounded range (values outside the bounds cannot occur), fit by direct maximum likelihood using truncnorm's truncated-normal density.
  • Both checked: a mixture of normal distributions, all sharing the same bounded range (e.g. a bimodal process where values below/above some limit cannot physically occur). This case has no ready-made CRAN function, so it is fit by direct maximum likelihood: a custom mixture-of-truncated-normals log-likelihood, optimized with stats::optim.

NOTE 1: mixtools does not support truncated data. If 'Truncate' is checked, the component-count selection below is ignored and the custom optimization path is used instead.
NOTE 2: The EM algorithm (mixtools) and direct optimization (truncated cases) can converge to a poor local optimum if started far from the true values, especially with more than 2 components. If results look wrong, or the optimizer reports a non-zero convergence code, try providing explicit starting mean values, or a different seed. The automatic component-count selection runs a few random restarts per component count for the same reason.
NOTE 3: Goodness-of-fit for mixture/truncated models here is assessed via AIC/BIC and the visual density overlay plot, not via the KS/CvM/AD p-value battery used in the 'Distribution Fit P-value' dialog - those tests assume a single, simple distributional form and are not well-defined for mixtures in the same way.
NOTE 4: For the truncated-mixture case, parameters are optimized on an unconstrained scale internally (log-scale for standard deviations, so they stay positive; a softmax/logit-style transform for mixing weights, so they stay positive and sum to 1) and converted back for display. AIC/BIC are computed manually from the optimized log-likelihood rather than via a package-provided method, since no single package function covers this exact model.

Usage
mixtools::normalmixEM(x, k, mu, sigma, lambda, maxit, epsilon)
truncnorm::dtruncnorm(x, a, b, mean, sd)
stats::optim(par, fn, method, control)
Arguments
  • x: the numeric variable selected above, with missing values removed.
  • k: the number of mixture components (fixed, or the value being tried during automatic selection).
  • mu, sigma, lambda: starting values for component means, standard deviations, and mixing weights (mixtools).
  • a, b: lower and upper truncation bounds (truncnorm); -Inf/Inf if left blank.
  • par, fn: starting parameter vector and the negative log-likelihood function being minimized (optim).
Value
A table of fitted component parameters (weight, mean, standard deviation per component), a table of model fit statistics (log-likelihood, AIC, BIC, N), a table of observation counts by most-likely component (mixture cases), and, if requested, a histogram with the fitted density (and each component's density) overlaid.
Package
mixtools, truncnorm
Help
help(normalmixEM, package = 'mixtools'), help(dtruncnorm, package = 'truncnorm')

A note on package choice
bbmle was considered for the truncated-mixture case (it gives a nicer summary()/confint() wrapper around a custom maximum-likelihood fit), but its interface expects a fixed, named set of parameters, which does not map cleanly onto a mixture whose parameter count changes with the number of components you choose. Rather than force that fit, this dialog uses stats::optim directly (always available, no extra dependency) with AIC/BIC computed manually from the optimized log-likelihood - the same approach already used elsewhere for models that do not natively report every fit statistic.

mclust was considered for the automatic "best number of components" selection (it does this search in a single, well-tested call). It was dropped in favor of looping mixtools::normalmixEM over each candidate component count and comparing BIC manually: mclust ships compiled Fortran source, and installing it requires a working compiler toolchain (Rtools on Windows, Xcode command-line tools on Mac) that is not always available, which can make installation fail outright on some machines. mixtools is pure R with no compiled dependencies, so this approach gives the same automatic behavior with a much more reliable install. The trade-off: mclust also compares equal-variance vs. unequal-variance component structures as part of its search, which this loop does not do (it always allows each component its own standard deviation), and mclust's initialization is generally a bit more robust than EM's random restarts at higher component counts.
